draft.title: Fitness testing
card: A fitness test measures one fitness component, such as aerobic power or flexibility. The result shows an athlete's strengths and weaknesses.
Results help set goals, such as a target score to reach by the end of a training block. Retesting later shows progress, which can motivate an athlete.
Use a standard, recognised test, so the method is the same each time and scores can be compared with earlier results or with others.
The test should match what the activity needs. A test of a component the activity hardly uses tells a coach little about performance.
draft.remember: Test what the activity needs, with a standard test, to find gaps, set goals and track progress.

a.q: Why would a coach retest an athlete at the end of a training block?
opts: To see whether the training has improved the scores
To replace the need for goals in the next training block
To show that the first test was done with the wrong method
To measure every fitness component with a single test
a.why: Retesting with the same standard test lets a coach compare scores and see progress, which can also motivate the athlete. It does not replace goals: the results are used to set new ones.
a.clue: Think about what two sets of scores can be compared to show.

b.q: Priya plays goalkeeper in netball-style team games that rely on short bursts of jumping and quick reactions. Her coach wants to find her weaknesses. Which test choice is best?
opts: A standard jump test, since the activity needs leg power
A standard long run, since all athletes need fitness
A new test the coach invents, since it suits Priya's team
A flexibility test only, since it is simple to run
b.why: A standard, recognised jump test measures leg power, which matches what the activity needs. A long run is standard but tests a component the activity hardly uses, so it tells the coach little. An invented test is not standard, so scores cannot be compared.
b.clue: The test must be both standard and matched to the activity.
